sessions.name: A
sessions.reply:
Here are some possible reasons, grouped by type. I haven't looked at the file.

**Weather and seasonal**
- **Late-summer heat.** September can stay hot, so air conditioning may have run longer than in the months before.
- **Early cold snap.** If you're in a cooler climate, electric heating may have started early.
- **Fewer cooling-friendly days.** Open windows and fans may have given way to AC.

**Household and behavior**
- **Back to school or work.** Kids at home, remote work, or more people in the house all raise daytime use.
- **Guests or a new occupant.**
- **More time indoors.** That means more lighting, cooking, TVs and computers.

**Appliances and equipment**
- **New or failing appliance.** An aging HVAC unit, a water heater, a fridge, or a dehumidifier can draw much more power as it fails.
- **New high-draw device.** An EV charger, space heater, pool pump, or hot tub would all show up.
- **Something left running.** A sump pump, a heat lamp, or a second fridge or freezer.

**Billing and rates**
- **Rate change.** Many utilities change rates in the fall, or have tiered or time-of-use pricing that moved.
- **Estimated read.** A catch-up bill after a few estimated ones can look like a spike.
- **Billing cycle length.** A 33-day cycle will cost more than a 28-day one.
- **New fees or taxes.** Fuel adjustments or a changed supply charge.

**Data quirks in the CSV**
- **Units.** kWh versus dollars, or a mix of the two.
- **Duplicate or misaligned rows.** Two bills falling in one month, or a missing August.
- **Date handling.** Billing periods may not line up with calendar months.

When you want to check, these would narrow it down fastest:
1. Look at usage (kWh) separately from cost. If kWh is flat but cost rose, the cause is rates or fees.
2. Compare September with September of last year, if the log goes back that far.
3. Look at the billing period start and end dates.

I can look at the file and test these if you'd like.

sessions.name: B
sessions.reply:
I wrote `utilities-plan.md` with a November 2026 budget of about **$223**, with a range of $196–$240.

| Category | Budget |
|---|---|
| Electricity | $120 |
| Water | $43 |
| Internet | $60 |

- **Electricity:** It was $88 in July and $93 in August, then jumped to $131 in September. I don't know why, so $120 sits between the three-month average ($104) and the September level.
- **Water and internet:** Water has stayed between $41 and $44, and internet is a flat $60.
- **Missing October data:** The log ends in September, so the estimate extrapolates from the spike. Add October and I can tighten it.
- **Limited history:** Three months of data gives no seasonal pattern, so winter heating could push electricity above the high case.

If the September jump was a one-off, the total would be closer to $195–200.
